newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Rocky road ahead for S.Korean bourse - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Rocky road ahead for S.Korean bourse - analysts.

text.p: The road ahead remains rocky for South Korean stocks despite hopes that the market's rapid climb at the end of last week signalled a recovery, analysts said.
South Korean investors showed wide mood swings last week, as fears over a weak economy battled with hopes the government would announce measures to boost the market, they said.
After falling to a 34-month low of 753.35 on Wednesday, the composite stock index clawed its way back by Saturday to close at 781.49, down 1.38 points on the day.
Some fund managers said the rise was a "dead cat bounce".
Yoon Park, an investment manager at Prudential Portfolio Managers in Hong Kong, said the rebound would not be sustained without fundamental changes in the econony.
Analysts expected the 800 level would be tough to break due to concern over the slowing economy, the sentencing to jail of major tycoons and a flood of new shares in the second half.
Negative economic statistics have continued to alarm investors, driving the index down 20 percent since April.

The trade deficit reached $10.36 billion in the year's first seven months, up 32 percent from last year's period as key exports such as semiconductors lagged. The current account shortfall for the same 1996 period was a record $11.66 billion
Gross domestic product (GDP) figures showed real growth of 6.7 percent in the second quarter versus 9.7 percent a year ago.
July industrial output slowed to eight percent from 15 in July, 1995 but was still up over June's meagre 3.8 percent gain.

Last week began on a down-note after the heads of several of the nation's largest conglomerates, including Daewoo, Jinro, Hanbo, and Dong Ah groups, were sentenced to jail for bribing former president Roh Tae-woo.

Fear of an oversupply of shares has hit sentiment. Five firms have been approved to hold initial public offerings in September and 12 more hope to list later in 1996. A large stake in state Korea Telecom could also be sold this year.
Soaring three-year corporate bond interest rates also haunted the market, reaching a year high of nearly 12.6 percent before stabilising on Friday at 12.22 percent.

Shares surged at the end of the week on rumours of an imminent announcement on the raising of the foreign shareholder ceiling. The government has said that the limit would be pushed up to 20 percent from the current 18 percent by year's end.
Analysts said bargain hunters were active on the belief that the market had been oversold.

"Everyone knew the current account deficit was going to be terrible," said Steven Lee at Shinyoung Securities. "But July's industrial output rise was better than June's and that just reminded investors that we're not having an economic meltdown."
But some fund managers remained skeptical.
"The problem with the South Korean market is that....there are no contrarians, and everyone rushes to bet the same way," said Choi Kwon-uk at the Citizens Investment Trust Co.
Government efforts to make the market more appealing did little to entice fund managers.

The finance ministry announced last week that from September it will ease controls on initial public offerings, allow margin trading in second tier shares, and expand the daily fluctuation limit of a stock to eight percent from the current six.
"I started reducing Korea's weighting in our funds from October 1995. From about seven percent, it's now less than three," said Park.

Despite the gloom, technical analysts saw the market near its bottom. Morgan Stanley Capital International plans to increase the weighting of South Korea in its Emerging Markets Free Index to 50 percent of the market capitalisation from 20 on Sept. 2.
